t.6.78.1: That greatly powerful night-roaming demon Indrajit, his horses slain, standing on the ground, became exceedingly enraged and blazed forth with fiery energy.
t.6.78.2: Those two bowmen, fiercely eager to slay each other with arrows, had sallied forth bent on victory, like two bull elephants in a forest.
t.6.78.3: Slaying one another, those rākṣasas and forest-dwelling monkeys, rushing together from every side, did not abandon their masters in battle.
t.6.78.4: Taking aim at Lakṣmaṇa and resorting to the utmost swiftness, he rained down showers of arrows, as Puraṃdara rains down showers of rain.
t.6.78.5: But Lakṣmaṇa, the tamer of foes, unperturbed, warded off that shower of arrows released by Indrajit, so very hard to withstand.
t.6.78.6: Deeming Lakṣmaṇa's armour impenetrable, Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa, utterly enraged, swiftly displaying his mastery of weapons, pierced Lakṣmaṇa in the forehead with three well-feathered arrows.
t.6.78.7: With those arrows lodged in his forehead, Raghunandana, who gloried in battle, shone at the forefront of the fight like a mountain with three peaks.
t.6.78.8: Though he was thus wounded by the rākṣasa's arrows in that great battle, Lakṣmaṇa swiftly struck him back with five shafts.
t.6.78.9: The two heroes Lakṣmaṇa and Indrajit, of terrible valour and armed with bows of great strength, struck each other with sharp-pointed arrows.
t.6.78.10: Those two bowmen, approaching each other, both with their minds set on victory, pierced one another in every limb with terrible arrows.
t.6.78.11: Enraged, Vibhīṣaṇa loosed with great force five arrows, like the touch of the thunderbolt, into the chest of him whose horses had been slain.
t.6.78.12: Those gold-feathered arrows, striking their mark, pierced through his body and, smeared with blood, became like great red serpents.
t.6.78.13: Enraged at his paternal uncle, the mighty Indrajit, standing in the midst of the rākṣasas, took up a superb arrow that had been given to him by Yama.
t.6.78.14: Seeing that mighty arrow fitted by him to the bow, the greatly splendid Lakṣmaṇa, of terrible valour, also took up another arrow.
t.6.78.15: It was what Kubera himself, of boundless spirit, had given in a dream: invincible and irresistible even to the gods and asuras together with Indra.
t.6.78.16: Those two excellent arrows, fitted by the two of them on their splendid bows and drawn back with force by the two heroes, blazed intensely with splendour.
t.6.78.17: Those two arrows, loosed from the two bows, lit up the sky as they flew; striking head against head, they collided with great force.
t.6.78.18: Those two, resembling great planets, collided with each other in the battle and, shattered into a hundred pieces, fell upon the earth.
t.6.78.19: Seeing their two arrows repelled at the forefront of battle, both of them, Lakṣmaṇa and Indrajit, were abashed and filled with rage.
t.6.78.21: A most tumultuous battle, like a wonder, took place between the two of them; the beings stationed in the sky gathered around Lakṣmaṇa.
t.6.78.20: Then Saumitri, greatly enraged, took up the Vāruṇa weapon; and standing firm in the fight, he released in battle the Raudra weapon, which could vanquish even great Indra.
t.6.78.22: In that terrible battle between the monkeys and the rākṣasas, resounding with fearsome cries, the sky shone, filled with many astonished beings.
t.6.78.23: The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the gandharvas, the garuḍas and the serpents, placing Śatakratu at their head, protected Lakṣmaṇa in the battle.
t.6.78.24: Then Rāvaṇa's younger brother fitted to his bow another excellent arrow, whose touch was like that of fire and which was terrible to the son of Rāvaṇa.
t.6.78.25: The hero took up an arrow, well-feathered, with a rounded shaft, well-jointed and firmly set, wrought with gold, an arrow that brings the body to its end.
t.6.78.27: That by which Śakra, the mighty and greatly splendid lord whose steeds are bay horses, conquered the Dānavas long ago in the war between the gods and the asuras.
t.6.78.26: It was hard to ward off and hard to withstand, bringing terror to the rākṣasas, like the venom of a poisonous serpent, and honored by the hosts of the gods.
t.6.78.28: Saumitri, the best of men, fixed upon the best of bows that best of arrows, the Aindra missile, never vanquished in battles.
t.6.78.30: Having fixed the arrow upon his excellent bow and drawing it back, the glorious Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words, which would accomplish his own purpose.
t.6.78.29: Fitting an enemy-rending arrow, the unassailable one drew back his bow. Bending the strung bow, he stood like Kāla, Time itself, at the destruction of the worlds.
t.6.78.31: If Rāma, son of Daśaratha, is righteous of soul and true to his word, and unrivaled in manly valor, then slay this son of Rāvaṇa.
t.6.78.32: Having spoken thus, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy warriors, drew that straight-flying arrow back to his ear and, joining it with the Aindra missile, released it in battle toward Indrajit.
t.6.78.33: That head of Indrajit, together with its helmet, glorious and with blazing earrings, was severed from his body and fell to the surface of the earth.
t.6.78.34: That great head of the rākṣasa's son, severed at the shoulders, gleaming like refined gold and drenched in blood, was seen lying on the ground.
t.6.78.35: Slain, the son of Rāvaṇa swiftly fell upon the earth, shattered, still clad in his armour, with his helmet and his bow.
t.6.78.36: Then all those vānaras, together with Vibhīṣaṇa, shouted aloud, rejoicing at his slaying, just as the devas had rejoiced at the slaying of Vṛtra.
t.6.78.37: Then in the sky there arose a great clamour of the beings, of the great-souled ṛṣis, and of the gandharvas and apsarases as well.
t.6.78.39: Being slain by the monkeys, those rākṣasas threw down their weapons, and all of them, bereft of their senses, ran off towards Laṅkā.
t.6.78.38: Realizing that he had fallen, that great rākṣasa army, being slaughtered by the triumphant monkeys, fled in all directions.
t.6.78.40: Terrified, the rākṣasas fled by hundreds in all directions, every one of them casting away his weapons, the spears, swords and battle-axes.
t.6.78.41: Some, terrified and harried by the monkeys, entered Laṅkā; some fell into the ocean, and some took refuge on the mountain.
t.6.78.42: Seeing Indrajit slain and lying upon the ground of the battlefield, not one among the thousands of rākṣasas was to be seen.
t.6.78.43: Just as the rays do not remain when the sun has gone to its setting, so, when he had fallen, those Rākṣasas fled in all directions.
t.6.78.44: Like the sun whose rays have been quenched, like a fire that has gone out, he of great splendor became, his life cast off and departed.
t.6.78.45: When the son of the lord of the rākṣasas had fallen, the world then became joyful, its many afflictions quelled and its enemy destroyed.
t.6.78.46: And when that rākṣasa of wicked deeds had been slain, the blessed Śakra, together with all the foremost of the gods, was filled with joy.
t.6.78.48: And all the gods, gandharvas and dānavas, gathered together, said: "Let the brāhmaṇas, free from fever and with their impurities quelled, now roam about."
t.6.78.47: When he who brought terror to all the worlds had fallen, the waters and the sky became pure, and the Daityas and Dānavas rejoiced and came there.
t.6.78.50: Vibhīṣaṇa, Hanūmān, and Jāmbavān, the leader of the bear troops, congratulating Lakṣmaṇa on his victory, also praised him.
t.6.78.49: Then the leaders of the monkey troops, thrilled with joy, rejoiced on the battlefield, seeing that bull among the Nairṛtas, whose might was unmatched, lying slain.
t.6.78.51: Hissing, shouting and roaring, the monkeys, having attained their aim, surrounded the scion of Raghu and stood in attendance upon him.
t.6.78.53: Embracing one another, the monkeys, their hearts filled with joy, told tales of every kind, high and low, arising from their refuge in Rāghava.
t.6.78.52: Then the monkeys, lashing their tails and slapping their arms, loudly proclaimed these words: “Lakṣmaṇa is victorious!”
t.6.78.54: Then, beholding that deed of Lakṣmaṇa in battle, so hard to accomplish, his dear friends rejoiced; and the gods, hearing that the enemy of Indra had been slain, attained the highest joy of heart.
